planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant out once soil has warmed into lean, sharply-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Set plants in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, since rich or soggy ground shortens this flax's lifespan considerably. Wiry, blue-gray stems carry a long succession of saucer-shaped, deep cornflower-blue flowers with a pale central eye through late spring and summer, each bloom lasting only a day but replaced continuously. Shear plants back by about a third after the first flush to encourage rebloom and keep the clump tidy, and avoid winter wet, which is the most common cause of loss in this otherwise reliably hardy Mediterranean native. Division is difficult, so propagate by seed or basal cuttings when renewing an aging planting.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant after last frost into gritty, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; good for rock gardens and raised beds.

directions: Plant in a raised bed, scree, or rock garden where drainage is sharp, as this low sub-shrubby flax resents winter dampness around its crown far more than cold itself. Clusters of bright golden-yellow, five-petaled flowers open atop short, woody-based stems with narrow blue-green leaves from early to midsummer, drawing bees steadily during bloom. Cut back lightly after flowering to maintain a tight mound and prevent the base from becoming woody and open in the center. It is short-lived in heavy or fertile soils, so keep a few seedlings or cuttings coming along as insurance.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost into disturbed, average garden soil in full to partial sun.

directions: Sow directly into average, well-worked soil after the ground has warmed, since this eastern North American native self-sows readily in meadows, roadsides, and old fields where it occurs naturally. The sticky, glandular-haired stems and leaves give the plant its common clammy name, and small tubular pink-purple flowers open along the upper stems from midsummer into fall. It is an important forage plant for Epeoloides pilosulus, a rare cuckoo bee specialist on Cuphea pollen, so leaving some plants unmowed through the season benefits local pollinator diversity. No deadheading is needed; simply let seed drop at season's end to maintain a self-renewing patch.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; self-sows readily once established.

directions: Grow in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun, where this Caucasus native forms a loose mound of finely dissected, silvery-gray foliage that contrasts well against darker-leaved border neighbors. Masses of small white, yellow-centered daisies cover the plant in early to midsummer on wiry stems, and the whole clump can look like a cloud of bloom from a distance. It tends to be short-lived, especially in rich or wet soils, but compensates by self-seeding freely, so allow a few spent flower heads to drop seed each year to keep a planting going. Shear plants back hard after flowering to tidy the foliage and discourage legginess.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; tolerates hard shearing.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, where this Chinese species forms a dense, fine-twigged shrub with notably smaller, narrower leaves than common or Chinese privet, making it a favored subject for both clipped hedges and bonsai training. Arching sprays of small white flowers open later in summer than most privets, followed by small blue-black berries that persist into winter and draw songbirds. Its fine texture and tight branching take repeated shearing well, holding a crisp formal line with less of the coarse, leggy regrowth seen in larger-leaved privet species. Watch for self-sown seedlings near fruiting plants and remove them promptly, as with other privets grown outside their native range.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
